questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Split in the Congress (1969)' refers to.
questions.a: The split in the Congress party in 1969 was a major political event in which the party divided into two factions -- the Congress (Organisation) led by the old guard (the Syndicate) and the Congress (Requisitionists) led by Indira Gandhi. The split arose from a power struggle between Indira Gandhi and the party's old leadership after the death of Lal Bahadur Shastri.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Split in the Congress (1969)'.
questions.a: The 1969 split had several causes and consequences: (1) after Shastri's death in 1966, Indira Gandhi became PM with the Syndicate's support, but tensions grew over policy; (2) the Syndicate backed the conservative candidate N. Sanjeeva Reddy for President in 1969, while Indira Gandhi supported V.V. Giri, who won; (3) the party formally split -- Indira's faction became Congress (R) and the old guard's became Congress (O); (4) Indira Gandhi adopted radical populist policies -- nationalisation of banks, abolition of privy purses -- to consolidate her position; (5) the split marked the end of the 'Congress system' of consensus politics.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Split in the Congress (1969)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Split in the Congress (1969)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The 1967 General Elections' refers to.
questions.a: The 1967 general elections were the fourth Lok Sabha elections, held in the context of severe economic hardship, food shortages, inflation and popular discontent. The Congress party's dominance was significantly reduced -- it lost seats in the Lok Sabha and in several states, and non-Congress governments were formed in many states for the first time.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The 1967 General Elections'.
questions.a: Key features of the 1967 elections: (1) context -- droughts, food crisis, devaluation of the rupee (1966), inflation and price rise; (2) the Congress won a reduced majority in the Lok Sabha (283 seats) and lost power in eight states; (3) non-Congress coalitions (Samyukta Vidhayak Dal, SVD) formed governments in states like Bihar, UP, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab; (4) the elections marked the emergence of coalition politics at the state level; (5) it signalled the beginning of the decline of the 'Congress system' of one-party dominance.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The 1967 General Elections' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The 1967 General Elections

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Coalition Governments after 1967' refers to.
questions.a: After the 1967 elections, non-Congress coalition governments -- known as Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments -- were formed in several Indian states. These coalitions brought together parties of diverse ideologies, from socialists and communists to the Jana Sangh and Swatantra Party, united mainly by their opposition to the Congress.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Coalition Governments after 1967'.
questions.a: Features of the post-1967 coalition governments: (1) they were formed in states like Bihar, UP, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab and West Bengal; (2) they united ideologically diverse parties -- socialists, communists, Jana Sangh, Swatantra and regional parties -- under the single aim of defeating the Congress; (3) they were often unstable due to ideological differences and factionalism; (4) many collapsed within a short period, leading to President's Rule; (5) despite instability, they demonstrated that non-Congress alternatives were possible and pioneered coalition politics in India.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Coalition Governments after 1967' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Coalition Governments after 1967

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Naxalite Movement' refers to.
questions.a: The Naxalite movement was a radical, armed peasant and communist insurgency that began in 1967 in the Naxalbari village of West Bengal's Darjeeling district. Led by Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, it advocated a violent revolution inspired by Maoist ideology to overthrow the Indian state and redistribute land to the peasantry.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Naxalite Movement'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the Naxalite movement: (1) origin -- the 1967 uprising in Naxalbari, West Bengal, by tribal peasants and radical communists; (2) leadership -- Charu Majumdar and Kanu Sanyal, who broke away from the CPI(M) to form the CPI(ML) in 1969; (3) ideology -- Maoist, advocating armed guerrilla war and immediate seizure of land; (4) social base -- landless labourers, tribals and poor peasants; (5) government response -- severe police and military crackdown; (6) significance -- it exposed the failure of land reforms and the deep poverty and dispossession in rural India, and it continues in parts of central India.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Naxalite Movement' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Naxalite Movement

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The JP Movement (1974-75)' refers to.
questions.a: The JP movement, also called the Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti) movement, was a mass movement launched in 1974-75 by Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) against the Congress government of Indira Gandhi. It began as a student agitation in Bihar against corruption and misgovernance and grew into a nationwide movement demanding the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The JP Movement (1974-75)'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the JP movement: (1) origin -- it began in 1974 as a student protest in Bihar against rising prices, unemployment and corruption; (2) leadership -- Jayaprakash Narayan, a respected socialist leader, was invited to lead it and gave it the call for 'Total Revolution' (sampoorna kranti) -- political, economic, social and moral; (3) the movement demanded the resignation of the Indira Gandhi government on charges of corruption; (4) it brought together opposition parties -- the Jana Sangh, socialists, Congress (O) and the CPI(M); (5) the Allahabad High Court's verdict (June 1975) invalidating Indira Gandhi's election gave the movement momentum; (6) the government responded by imposing the Emergency in June 1975.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The JP Movement (1974-75)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The JP Movement (1974-75)

concepts.title: Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections' refers to.
questions.a: The restoration of democracy in 1977 followed the end of the Emergency. Indira Gandhi called elections for March 1977, expecting to win, but the opposition -- united as the Janata Party -- won a decisive victory. The Congress was routed, and Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress Prime Minister, marking the restoration of democratic rule.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the 1977 elections and restoration: (1) Indira Gandhi ended the Emergency and called elections in March 1977; (2) the opposition parties -- Congress (O), Jana Sangh, socialists and Bharatiya Lok Dal -- merged to form the Janata Party under JP's guidance; (3) the Janata Party won 295 seats and the Congress was reduced to 154 seats; Indira Gandhi and Sanjay Gandhi lost their seats; (4) Morarji Desai became PM; (5) the new government released political prisoners, restored press freedom, and repealed the Emergency provisions; (6) the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed many changes of the 42nd Amendment and strengthened safeguards against future emergencies.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Restoration of Democracy and the 1977 Elections

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Janata Party Government' refers to.
questions.a: The Janata Party government (1977-79) was India's first non-Congress government at the Centre, led by Prime Minister Morarji Desai. Formed by a merger of four opposition parties, it came to power on the promise of restoring democracy but collapsed within two-and-a-half years due to internal differences and factionalism.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Janata Party Government'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the Janata Party government: (1) formation -- a merger of the Congress (O), Jana Sangh, Bharatiya Lok Dal and socialists, led by Morarji Desai as PM; (2) achievements -- restoration of democratic freedoms, release of political prisoners, the 44th Amendment reversing the 42nd, and the Mandal Commission (1979) on backward classes; (3) weaknesses -- ideological differences (especially over the 'dual membership' issue of Jana Sangh members), personal rivalries between Morarji Desai, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram; (4) collapse -- Morarji Desai resigned in 1979, Charan Singh formed a short-lived government that fell without facing Parliament, leading to fresh elections in 1980; (5) the Janata experiment showed both the possibility and the fragility of non-Congress governments.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Janata Party Government' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Janata Party Government

concepts.title: The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)' refers to.
questions.a: The return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress to power in 1980 followed the collapse of the Janata Party government. In the 1980 Lok Sabha elections, the Congress (I) won a decisive victory, and Indira Gandhi returned as Prime Minister, marking the restoration of Congress dominance after the interlude of the Janata Party.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)'.
questions.a: Key aspects of the 1980 return: (1) context -- the collapse of the Janata Party government in 1979 due to internal divisions; (2) the 1980 elections -- the Congress (I) won 353 seats, returning to power; (3) factors for victory -- the disunity and infighting of the Janata Party, the failure of the Janata government to deliver, and Indira Gandhi's campaign emphasising stability; (4) consequences -- restoration of Congress dominance, centralisation of power, and the rise of Sanjay Gandhi's influence; (5) the period also saw the rise of regional parties and the beginning of a new phase of coalition politics in the longer term.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: The Return of Indira Gandhi and the Congress (1980)
